csharp-15-unions.title: C# 15: union types & closed hierarchies
csharp-15-unions.shortDescription: Model "exactly one of these types" natively, with an exhaustive switch checked by the compiler.

content.mainTitle: C# 15: union types and closed hierarchies
content.intro: Modeling a value that is "exactly one of these three types" has always required workarounds in C#: an abstract class plus sealed classes, an enum plus optional fields, or a NuGet dependency such as OneOf. C# 15 finally ships two native building blocks: the union keyword and closed hierarchies. The compiler now knows the full list of cases, so your switch becomes exhaustive without a catch-all arm.
content.summary: C# 15 union types and closed hierarchies let you model a fixed choice between several types, with exhaustive pattern matching verified at compile time.

whyUnions.title: The problem today
whyUnions.description: Take a payment: it is approved, declined, or pending. Each case carries different data. In C# 14 you write an abstract class with one sealed class per case. It works, but the compiler can never prove your case list is complete: any assembly can derive a fourth case.
whyUnions.painTitle: What it costs day to day
painItems: A mandatory catch-all arm in every switch, otherwise warning CS8509
Adding a case breaks no build: missed spots surface in production
A lot of ceremony for what is just a choice between three shapes
Common alternative: a NuGet dependency (OneOf) that forces its own calling style
whyUnions.codeCaption: The classic modeling approach, with its defensive catch-all arm.

unions.title: Union types
unions.description: The union keyword declares a type whose value is exactly one of the listed types. The declaration fits on one line and reuses types you already defined: records, classes, structs.
unions.declarationDescription: The three records stay normal types, usable elsewhere. The union only declares the fixed choice between them.
unions.usageDescription: Conversion from each case is implicit, and the switch no longer needs a catch-all arm: the compiler knows the complete case list.

closed.title: Closed hierarchies
closed.description: The closed modifier applies to a base class or record: only the declaring assembly can derive from it. Prefer this variant when your cases share common members or a real inheritance relationship, while union fits independent types better.
closed.usageTitle: Exhaustive switch over a closed hierarchy
closed.usageDescription: Add a new state in the assembly and this method stops compiling: exactly the safety net you want on a state machine.
closed.note: union and closed are complementary: union assembles independent types, closed locks down an existing hierarchy. Both give the compiler the same exhaustiveness guarantee.

matching.title: Exhaustive pattern matching
matching.description: A union composes with everything pattern matching has done since C# 8: property patterns, nested type patterns, relational patterns. The difference is that exhaustiveness is now verified.
rulesItems: Without a catch-all arm, the compiler requires one arm per union case
A more specific arm (property pattern) does not count as covering the whole case: keep a general arm
Order still matters: most specific first, most general last
Adding a case to the union turns every incomplete switch into a compile error

setup.title: Enabling C# 15
setup.description: C# 15 ships with .NET 11. At the time of writing this tip the release is still in preview: .NET 11 GA is announced for November 10, 2026. You need the .NET 11 SDK and LangVersion set to preview.
statusItems: Compiler support for unions shipped in .NET 11 Preview 2
IDE support (completion, refactorings) arrived in Preview 3
Visual Studio 2026 Insiders or a recent JetBrains Rider recommended
Treat it as a preview: the syntax may still change before GA
alsoItems: Collection expression arguments: pass a capacity or comparer with the with(...) syntax
Extension indexers: declare an indexer inside an extension block
Labeled break and continue, to explicitly target an enclosing loop
Relaxed unsafe requirements on some pointer operations

useCases.title: Concrete use cases
useCases.description: Unions shine wherever an operation has several legitimate outcomes you do not want to express as an exception or as a boolean plus a message.
items: Domain results: replace a hand-rolled Result<T> or a (bool Success, string Error) pair with an explicit choice between Success, ValidationFailed and NotAuthorized
State machines: order Draft, Paid, Shipped, Cancelled, with a switch that breaks at compile time when a state is added
Parsing and validation: ParseOk, ParseSyntaxError, ParseOutOfRange, each carrying its own data
API responses and anti-corruption layers: translate an HTTP code into typed cases instead of numeric code checks
Message handlers: a handler returning Handled, Rejected or Retry, without control-flow exceptions

comparison.title: Pros and cons versus OneOf
comparison.description: The current reference for unions in C# is the OneOf library. It works from C# 9 and is still installed in many projects. Here is how the two compare.
prosItems: No NuGet dependency, no fixed-arity generic type (OneOf<T0, T1, T2>...)
The regular switch works: no lambda-based Match API to learn
Exhaustiveness verified by the compiler, with native error messages
Composes with existing pattern matching: property patterns, nesting, relational patterns
More readable signatures: PaymentResult instead of OneOf<Approved, Declined, Pending>
consItems: OneOf runs on .NET 8 LTS today; unions require .NET 11, not an LTS, GA only on November 10, 2026
The ecosystem has not caught up: System.Text.Json serialization, EF Core mapping, OpenAPI generators need case-by-case checks
OneOf offers battle-tested helpers (Match, Switch, TryPickT0) that native unions leave to you
Migrating an existing codebase means touching every affected public signature
IDE tooling for unions is still young: expect rough edges in preview
comparison.verdict: In practice: on a new service targeting .NET 11, go straight to native unions. On a .NET 8 or .NET 10 codebase in production, keep OneOf and hide unions behind your domain types so the migration stays mechanical when the time comes.
